entries.title: Creole tomato
entries.summary: A Louisiana-grown tomato picked ripe, not a single variety: the name comes from the river-soil farms of St. Bernard and Plaquemines parishes. Sweet, sharp and juicy, it is a summer crop, eaten raw and cooked into the city's tomato dishes.
entries.guest: Creole tomatoes are Louisiana's summer tomatoes, picked ripe on the vine: juicy, sweet and a little sharp. On the tostada they are served raw with heirlooms and burrata.

paras: A Creole tomato is not one variety. It is a tomato grown in Louisiana, left to ripen on the vine and sold close to home. The name belongs first to the growers of St. Bernard and Plaquemines parishes, below New Orleans on the lower Mississippi, who long sold their fruit as Creole and credited the rich alluvial soil, the silt the river laid down over centuries, for a flavour they said no other tomato had. In the early 1900s tomatoes from the river parishes upstream were simply called Creole too.

Why it matters: a tomato picked ripe tastes of sugar and acid together, sweet, sharp and juicy, with a thin, soft skin. That softness means it bruises easily and will not travel far, so it is a local, seasonal thing, and the kitchen treats it as a visitor from the farm rather than a staple.

LSU muddied the name in 1969, when its researcher Teme Hernandez released a variety actually called Creole. It yielded poorly and the university kept no seed stock of it, so a plant sold as Creole today may not be the original, and the word still means a Louisiana tomato picked ripe, not one cultivar. The season runs from late spring into summer, with the main crop from late May into July, and the city marks it each June at the French Market's Creole Tomato Festival, a celebration of the tomatoes and the farmers who grow them.

Buy by smell and weight: a ripe Creole tomato smells green and sweet at the stem, feels heavy for its size and gives a little under the thumb. Keep whole ripe tomatoes at room temperature, stem side down and out of the sun, and use them within a day or two. Never chill a whole ripe tomato: below about 10°C (50°F) the flesh turns mealy and the aroma fades. Once it is cut, though, it goes into the cold, at 5°C (41°F) or below, covered and labelled, because the FDA Food Code treats cut tomatoes as a food that needs temperature control.

Raw is where a Creole tomato shines. Slice it thick with a sharp or serrated knife, salt it just before it goes out, and add black pepper and a thread of good oil; salt it too early and the juice runs across the plate. In New Orleans it goes into sandwiches, as the tomato in a po-boy dressed with lettuce, tomato, pickles and mayonnaise, and into plain tomato salads with onion and herbs.

Cooked, it is the base of Creole sauce, of shrimp Creole and of a Creole courtbouillon, fish stewed in a tomato and roux gravy. To peel a tomato for cooking, cut a shallow cross in the base, drop it into boiling water for 10 to 20 seconds, refresh it in iced water and slip off the skin; peeled, seeded and diced, it becomes concassé. Out of season a good tinned plum tomato, packed ripe, does more for a sauce than a pale winter tomato bought fresh.

On the Creole Tomato Tostada, a dinner starter, Creole tomatoes are mixed with Louisiana heirloom tomatoes and served raw and simply, with creamy burrata on a crisp okra tostada the kitchen makes in house. Smoked tomato water, the clear juice of strained tomatoes with a gentle smoke, is poured around last so the shell stays crisp for the first bites. The dish follows the season and changes when the tomatoes finish. Never name a farm or a parish for tonight's tomatoes unless the kitchen says so at lineup.

Guests often ask whether Creole is a breed of tomato. The honest answer is that the word is older than the 1969 variety and means local and vine-ripened. Sell the tostada as a light first course while the season lasts, and tell the guest to eat it soon after it lands, because the crunch fades within minutes. Any question about what the tostada itself is made with goes to the kitchen.

cards.front: Is a Creole tomato a single variety?
cards.back: No. It is a Louisiana-grown tomato picked ripe on the vine; the name is a growers' word older than any one variety.

cards.front: Which parishes gave the Creole tomato its name?
cards.back: St. Bernard and Plaquemines, below New Orleans, whose growers sold their tomatoes as Creole and credited the rich river soil.

cards.front: What happened in 1969 to confuse the name Creole tomato?
cards.back: LSU released a variety called Creole, but the growers' word is older, and the university kept no seed stock of it, so the name still means a Louisiana tomato picked ripe.

cards.front: When are Creole tomatoes in season, and how does the city mark it?
cards.back: Late spring into summer, the main crop from late May into July, celebrated each June at the French Market's Creole Tomato Festival.

cards.front: Why are Creole tomatoes prized over tomatoes shipped from far away?
cards.back: They ripen on the vine, so they are sweet, sharp and juicy; the soft skin that comes with ripeness means they do not travel far.

cards.front: Why is a whole ripe tomato never kept in the fridge?
cards.back: Below about 10°C (50°F) its flesh turns mealy and its aroma fades; keep it at room temperature, stem side down.

cards.front: How is a cut tomato kept in the kitchen?
cards.back: Cold, at 5°C (41°F) or below, covered and labelled: the FDA Food Code treats cut tomatoes as a food that needs temperature control.

cards.front: When do you salt sliced raw tomatoes, and why then?
cards.back: Just before they go out: salt draws out the juice, so salting early leaves the slices sitting in a watery plate.

cards.front: How do you peel a tomato for a sauce?
cards.back: Score a shallow cross in the base, blanch it 10 to 20 seconds in boiling water, refresh it in iced water, then slip off the skin.

cards.front: What stands in for Creole tomatoes in a sauce out of season?
cards.back: A good tinned plum tomato, packed ripe, which does more for a Creole sauce than a pale winter tomato bought fresh.

cards.front: How are Creole tomatoes served on the Creole Tomato Tostada?
cards.back: Raw, mixed with Louisiana heirlooms, with burrata on a crisp okra tostada and smoked tomato water poured around last.

cards.front: What do you tell a guest about eating the tostada?
cards.back: Eat it soon after it lands: the smoked tomato water goes on last, and the crunch of the okra tostada fades within minutes.

entries.title: Gulf shrimp
entries.summary: Wild shrimp from the Gulf coast, mostly brown and white, are the backbone of New Orleans cooking. Know the species and their seasons, read the count per pound, cook them briefly and say plainly where they come from.
entries.guest: On the Shrimp & Grits these are wild Louisiana shrimp, from one of the country's great shrimp states: sweet and firm, cooked only until they turn pink.

paras: Gulf shrimp are the wild shrimp caught in the bays, passes and open water of the Gulf coast, and they are the backbone of New Orleans cooking: gumbo, Creole sauce, étouffée (shrimp smothered in a thick sauce over rice), rémoulade (a sharp, spiced cold sauce) and fried shrimp. Louisiana is one of the country's largest shrimp producers, and shrimp is its most valuable commercial fishery.

Three species matter. Brown shrimp come in spring and early summer, in Louisiana's season roughly May to July, and taste a little more of iodine and the sea. White shrimp come in late summer and autumn, roughly mid-August to mid-December, and are sweeter and milder. Pink shrimp, caught mostly off Florida, are mild and sweet and often pinkish even raw. The state opens each area on its biologists' advice.

Shrimp are sold by count: how many make a pound (450 g). U-15 means under 15 to the pound; 16/20 means 16 to 20; 21/25 means 21 to 25. The smaller the number, the larger the shrimp. Words such as jumbo mean different things from one seller to the next, so a cook orders by count; a head-on count differs from a tail count. Look for firm, sweet-smelling shrimp with shells that cling; a smell of ammonia, slime or black spots at the head mean age.

Almost 90 per cent of the shrimp eaten in the United States is imported, much of it farmed in Asia and Latin America. Wild Gulf shrimp taste of the water they lived in and keep the boats and docks of the coast working, which is why a menu that names Louisiana or Gulf shrimp is making a claim worth saying aloud. Louisiana law agrees: since 2019 a restaurant serving imported shrimp or crawfish must say so, on its menu or, where it has none, on a posted sign.

Head-on shrimp keep more flavour, and New Orleans barbecue shrimp is made with them, the fat in the heads enriching the sauce. The heads also spoil first, so head-on shrimp are bought fresh and cooked soon. Save every head and shell for the shrimp stock the Creole kitchen builds its gumbo, étouffée and sauces on: cook them gently in a little oil or butter, stirring, until pink and fragrant, cover with cold water, add onion, celery and bay, simmer gently for 20 to 30 minutes and strain. Longer, and the stock turns bitter and cloudy. To prepare the tails, peel them, run a knife down the back and lift out the dark vein, the gut, which can carry grit.

Shrimp cook in a couple of minutes. Raw, they are grey and translucent; cooked, they turn pink and opaque and curl into a loose C. Pushed further they tighten into an O and turn rubbery: C for cooked, O for overdone. The curl is only a hint, since a split or butterflied shrimp cannot curl; the real test is opaque flesh at the thickest part, and the FDA Food Code's cooking figure for seafood is 63°C (145°F). In a gumbo or a sauce, shrimp go in at the very end.

The fishery is old and many-voiced. By the 1880s the marshes south of New Orleans held villages on stilts around raised platforms where shrimp were dried in the sun for markets in Asia, and at the peak, between 1900 and 1915, there were at least 95 of them. Chinese merchants ran much of the trade, and the shrimpers were Filipino, Chinese, Croatian, Isleño, Cajun, Creole and more.

Shrimp go into the Seafood Gumbo with crab and oysters, top the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits in a Creole sauce with tasso, come as bite-size Popcorn Shrimp with a Crystal gastrique in the Roost, and are fried with French fries on the children's dinner. Use the menu's words: Louisiana shrimp on the Shrimp & Grits and the Popcorn Shrimp, Gulf shrimp on the children's dinner plate. The children's breakfast also has popcorn shrimp with Brabant potatoes; its menu line prints no origin, so say popcorn shrimp and leave the source to the kitchen. Never say all our shrimp are Louisiana, and if a guest asks brown or white, ask the kitchen rather than guess.

On the Shrimp & Grits and the Popcorn Shrimp, where the menu prints Louisiana, a true and easy line: “These are wild Louisiana shrimp, from one of the largest shrimp fisheries in the country.” Shellfish questions always go to the kitchen, never a guess from the floor.

faults.fault: Rubbery shrimp curled into a tight O
faults.cause: Cooked too long, or left simmering in a gumbo or sauce.
faults.fix: Pull them as soon as the thickest part turns opaque in a loose C, and add them to a sauce at the very end.

faults.cause: Old shrimp, or head-on shrimp kept too long before cooking.
faults.fix: Buy by smell and firmness, and cook head-on shrimp soon after they arrive.

faults.cause: The shells were boiled hard or simmered far too long.
faults.fix: Simmer gently for 20 to 30 minutes, then strain at once.

faults.cause: The vein, the gut along the back, was left in.
faults.fix: Run a knife down the back after peeling and lift the vein out.

Bite-size fried Louisiana shrimp, crunchy outside and sweet inside, served in the Roost with a Crystal gastrique, a sweet and sour sauce made with the New Orleans hot sauce.

cards.front: Which two species carry Louisiana's shrimp fishery?
cards.back: Brown shrimp, in spring and early summer, and white shrimp, in late summer and autumn; pink shrimp come mostly from Florida.

cards.front: How do brown and white shrimp differ on the plate?
cards.back: Brown shrimp taste a little more of iodine and the sea; white shrimp are sweeter and milder.

cards.front: When do Louisiana's brown and white shrimp seasons run?
cards.back: Brown roughly May to July; white roughly mid-August to mid-December, each area opened by the state on its biologists' advice.

cards.front: What does 16/20 on a case of shrimp mean?
cards.back: Between 16 and 20 shrimp make a pound (450 g); the smaller the number, the larger the shrimp.

cards.front: What does U-15 mean on a case of shrimp?
cards.back: Under 15 shrimp to the pound (450 g): very large shrimp, bigger than 16/20 or 21/25.

cards.front: Why buy head-on shrimp, and what is the catch?
cards.back: The heads carry fat and flavour for barbecue shrimp and stock, but they spoil first, so head-on shrimp are cooked soon after they arrive.

cards.front: How do you make stock from shrimp heads and shells?
cards.back: Cook them gently in a little fat until pink, cover with cold water, add onion, celery and bay, simmer gently for 20 to 30 minutes, then strain.

cards.front: How do you read doneness in a shrimp?
cards.back: Grey and translucent turns pink and opaque, curled into a loose C; a tight O means overcooked. The thickest part should be opaque.

cards.front: What is the vein in a shrimp, and why take it out?
cards.back: It is the gut running down the back; it can carry grit, so it is lifted out with the tip of a knife after peeling.

cards.front: Why does a menu name Louisiana or Gulf shrimp?
cards.back: Almost 90 per cent of US shrimp is imported, much of it farmed; wild local shrimp is a real claim, and Louisiana law requires notice of imports.

cards.front: What were the shrimp-drying platforms of the Louisiana marsh?

entries.title: Crawfish
entries.summary: Crawfish are small freshwater crustaceans, mostly red swamp crawfish, farmed in Louisiana's rice fields and trapped wild in the Atchafalaya Basin. They are boiled whole in spring, and their tail meat and golden fat carry étouffée, bisque and pies all year.
entries.guest: Crawfish are little freshwater cousins of the lobster and a Louisiana spring tradition. At the Roost they fill the Crawfish Meat Pies, served with a chive rémoulade for dipping.

paras: Crawfish are freshwater crustaceans that look like lobsters no longer than a hand, and in Louisiana they are a season, a party and a pantry staple at once. Say crawfish: crayfish is the textbook word, and crawdad belongs to other parts of the country. Most of what Louisiana sells is the red swamp crawfish, with the white river crawfish a smaller share of the catch.

Louisiana grows nearly all of the country's crawfish. Most are farmed, in ponds and above all in rice fields: crawfish are stocked into the growing rice in late spring and burrow through the summer, and once the rice is harvested and the stubble regrows, the fields are flooded again in autumn, so the same clay soil gives a second crop from late autumn into spring. The rest are trapped wild in the Atchafalaya Basin, the largest river swamp in the United States.

The season runs roughly January to June and is at its best in spring, when the crawfish are big and both the farms and the basin are producing; wild crawfish usually reach market size in April, May and June. Live crawfish are bought by the sack, lively and smelling of clean water, never of ammonia. The rest of the year the kitchen uses frozen tail meat, peeled and cooked, sold in 450 g (1 lb) packs and often with the fat. It takes 2.7 to 3.2 kg (6 to 7 lb) of live crawfish to give 450 g (1 lb) of tails, a yield of about 15 per cent, which is why peeled tails are dear.

Imported tail meat, much of it from China, is usually cheaper and often washed of most of its fat, and many cooks find it blander and softer. Since 2019 Louisiana law has required a restaurant serving imported crawfish or shrimp to say so, on its menu or, where it has none, on a posted sign, so the label is a question of flavour and of honesty: a guest who asks deserves the kitchen's answer, never a guess.

The boil is the spring ritual. Live crawfish are rinsed in clean water until it runs clear, which washes off mud and grit. As they rinse, pick out and throw away any that are dead: limp and still, or floating. What most people call purging is this rinse: LSU AgCenter research found that emptying the gut takes a 12 to 24 hour soak in fresh water, and that salt in the rinse adds little.

A big pot of water is seasoned fiercely into a court-bouillon, the French kitchen's name for a short, quickly made seasoned cooking liquid (not the Creole fish stew called courtbouillon): salt, cayenne, lemons, onions, garlic and bay, or a ready-made boil, brought to a rolling boil. Potatoes go in first, then corn, then the crawfish, which cook only a few minutes once the pot returns to the boil. Then the heat goes off and they soak for 15 to 30 minutes: the soak, not the boil, is where they drink in the seasoning.

In the kitchen the prize is the tail meat and the fat, the golden paste in the head. It is not fat at all but the hepatopancreas, the organ that does the work of liver and pancreas, and it carries the deep, rich flavour of étouffée, crawfish or shrimp smothered in a thick sauce and served over rice; of bisque, a rich, smooth soup; and of crawfish pie. Good cooks scrape every bit into the pot. It turns quickly, so tails packed with fat are kept cold and used fast.

In the Roost, the Crawfish Meat Pies are the most Louisiana snack on the Bubbles at Brennan's list: savoury meat pies filled with crawfish, served with a chive rémoulade for dipping. They follow Louisiana's meat pie tradition, best known from Natchitoches, where a fried half-moon of pastry holds seasoned meat. The menu does not print Louisiana for the crawfish, and the pastry, the filling and the number in an order are not printed either, so each is a question for the kitchen.

Offer the pies to a visitor who wants a local taste with a glass of bubbles. A true line about Louisiana crawfish: most are farmed, many of them in rice fields as a second crop after the rice harvest. A straight tail on a boiled crawfish does not prove it was dead before cooking, whatever a guest has heard. Shellfish questions always go to the kitchen.

ratios.label: Live crawfish to peeled tail meat
ratios.value: 2.7 to 3.2 kg (6 to 7 lb) live for 450 g (1 lb) of tails, about 15 per cent

faults.cause: A light hand with the seasoning, or crawfish lifted straight out after the boil with no soak.
faults.fix: Season the pot fiercely, and after a few minutes at the boil turn off the heat and let them soak for 15 to 30 minutes.

faults.fault: Mushy tails that stick in the shell
faults.cause: Boiled too long, or left cooking on in a pot that stayed too hot.
faults.fix: Boil only a few minutes once the pot returns to the boil, then take the heat off for the soak.

faults.cause: The live crawfish went into the pot without a proper rinse.
faults.fix: Rinse them in clean water until it runs clear before they go in.

faults.fault: A flat étouffée or pie filling
faults.cause: Tail meat washed of its fat, or the fat left behind in the heads.
faults.fix: Use tails packed with their fat, and scrape the fat into the pot.

faults.fault: A soft, off-smelling tail in the pile
faults.cause: Dead crawfish went into the pot with the live ones.
faults.fix: Cull the sack as it is rinsed, throwing out any limp or still crawfish before the boil.

cards.front: What are crawfish, and which species does Louisiana mostly sell?
cards.back: Freshwater crustaceans like small lobsters; mostly red swamp crawfish, with white river crawfish a smaller share of the catch.

cards.front: How are most Louisiana crawfish farmed?
cards.back: In rice fields: stocked into the growing rice in spring, then flooded again in autumn after the harvest, so the same clay soil gives a second crop through the cool months.

cards.front: Where are wild Louisiana crawfish trapped?
cards.back: In the Atchafalaya Basin, the largest river swamp in the United States; wild crawfish usually reach market size in April, May and June.

cards.front: When is crawfish season in Louisiana?
cards.back: Roughly January to June, at its best in spring; frozen tail meat serves the kitchen the rest of the year.

cards.front: What does purging live crawfish really do?
cards.back: The rinse washes off mud and grit; emptying the gut takes a 12 to 24 hour freshwater soak, and salt in the rinse adds little.

cards.front: In what order do potatoes, corn and crawfish go into the boil?
cards.back: Potatoes first, because they take longest, then corn, then the crawfish for a short boil and a long soak.

cards.front: Where do boiled crawfish take on their seasoning?
cards.back: In the soak: after a few minutes at the boil the heat goes off and they sit 15 to 30 minutes in the seasoned liquor.

cards.front: What is crawfish fat?
cards.back: Not fat but the hepatopancreas, the golden organ in the head that works as liver and pancreas; it gives étouffée and pies their rich flavour.

cards.front: How much live crawfish gives 450 g (1 lb) of peeled tails?
cards.back: About 2.7 to 3.2 kg (6 to 7 lb), a yield of roughly 15 per cent, which is why peeled tails are dear.

cards.front: Why does the label on crawfish tail meat matter?
cards.back: Imported tails, much of them from China, are often washed of fat and blander, and Louisiana law requires a menu notice, or a posted sign where there is no menu, for imported crawfish.

cards.front: Does a straight tail prove a boiled crawfish was dead before cooking?
cards.back: No. LSU AgCenter found tail curl is not a reliable sign; what matters is lively crawfish going into the pot.

cards.front: How are crawfish served at Brennan's?
cards.back: In the Roost's Crawfish Meat Pies with a chive rémoulade; whether the tails are Louisiana crawfish is a question for the kitchen.

questions.q: Which species makes up most of Louisiana's crawfish harvest?
distractors: White river crawfish
Signal crayfish
Spiny lobster
questions.why: The red swamp crawfish dominates both the farms and the wild catch; the white river crawfish is the smaller second species.

questions.q: Which crop do Louisiana farmers most often rotate with crawfish?
distractors: Sugar cane
Cotton
Sweet potatoes
questions.why: Crawfish stocked into the growing rice burrow through the summer; after the harvest the fields are flooded again, so the same clay soil gives a second crop.

questions.q: When is Louisiana crawfish season at its best?
distractors: Late autumn
High summer
Midwinter
questions.why: The season runs roughly January to June, and spring brings big crawfish from both the farms and the Atchafalaya Basin.

questions.q: After a short boil, why do cooks turn off the heat and leave the crawfish in the pot?
distractors: The shells need time to turn red
It lets the potatoes catch up
It drains the fat out of the heads
questions.why: The crawfish cook in minutes; the 15 to 30 minute soak off the heat is where the seasoning goes in while the tails stay firm.

questions.q: What did LSU AgCenter research find about adding salt to the crawfish purge?
questions.answer: It adds little; clean water does the rinsing
distractors: It empties the gut in ten minutes
It is needed before any crawfish can boil
It makes the tails curl more tightly
questions.why: A rinse in clean water removes mud and grit; only a 12 to 24 hour freshwater soak empties the gut, and salt adds little.

questions.q: Which goes into the crawfish boil first?
distractors: Crawfish
Corn
A bag of ice
questions.why: Potatoes take longest, so they go in first, then corn, then the crawfish for a few minutes at the boil before the soak.

questions.q: What is the golden crawfish fat prized in étouffée?
distractors: Butter added at the packing house
Roe carried under the tail
Fat rendered from the tail meat
questions.why: The fat is the hepatopancreas, which does the work of liver and pancreas; it carries the rich flavour cooks scrape into the pot.

questions.q: Roughly what share of a live crawfish's weight ends up as peeled tail meat?
distractors: About half
About 75 per cent
About 40 per cent
questions.why: It takes about 2.7 to 3.2 kg (6 to 7 lb) of live crawfish for 450 g (1 lb) of tails, which explains the price of peeled meat.

questions.q: Since 2019, what must a Louisiana restaurant do if it serves imported crawfish?
distractors: Tell a guest only if they ask
Label the bags in the walk-in
Buy only from licensed importers
questions.why: Louisiana law requires a menu notice, or a sign where there is no menu, for imported crawfish or shrimp, which is why the label on tail meat matters to a guest.

questions.q: What is served with the Crawfish Meat Pies in the Roost?
distractors: A Crystal gastrique
A brown butter vinaigrette
A preserved Fresno chilli mignonette
questions.why: The Roost's Crawfish Meat Pies come with a chive rémoulade; the gastrique belongs to the Popcorn Shrimp, the vinaigrette to the crab claws and the mignonette to the raw oysters.

entries.title: Blue crab and lump crabmeat
entries.summary: The blue crab of the Gulf and Atlantic, Louisiana's great crab catch, reaches the kitchen as picked meat sold by grade, as claws and as soft-shells. Know the grades, pick the meat over and fold it gently so the lumps stay whole.
entries.guest: That's Louisiana lump crab: sweet, hand-picked blue crab from the state that catches more of it than any other, warmed gently so it stays tender.

paras: The blue crab, Callinectes sapidus, the beautiful savoury swimmer, lives in the brackish bays and marshes of the Gulf and the Atlantic, where river water meets the sea. It takes its name from the blue of its claws and turns red when cooked. Louisiana runs the largest blue crab fishery in the country and lands about a quarter of the national catch. Most of it is cooked and picked by hand, and the meat reaches kitchens already cooked and chilled, sold by grade, which is why a cook only ever warms crabmeat through, gently, even inside a crab cake or a gratin, and never cooks it hard.

Jumbo lump is the two large muscles that drive the swimming legs, whole, white and costly, kept for dishes where the crab is the show. Lump is large body pieces and broken jumbo, the grade just below jumbo lump. Backfin is smaller flakes of lump with some white body meat. Special is the white flake from the body, good for crab cakes, dips and stuffings. Claw meat is darker, pinkish brown, firmer and sweeter, with a stronger flavour, and it costs least. New Orleans seafood counters often sell just three, jumbo lump, backfin lump and claw, so read each seller's own description of what its backfin lump holds.

Fresh-picked crabmeat keeps only days; pasteurised crabmeat, sealed and heated in its tub, keeps far longer unopened, and the kitchen's labels decide the use-by. Cocktail claws are claws with the shell cracked away and the pincer left on as a handle. They come cooked and are served cold with a sauce for dipping, or warmed in butter; cooked again, the meat tightens onto the cartilage and will not pull free.

Even good crabmeat hides shell and cartilage. To pick it over, spread it in a thin layer on a cold tray and run your fingertips lightly through it, feeling for hard flakes and lifting them out without squeezing the meat; some kitchens use an ultraviolet lamp, under which shell glows. Then treat it gently. Fold lump into a sauce, a stuffing or a filling with a spatula at the very end, lifting from beneath rather than stirring, so the pieces stay whole, and warm it through in butter or sauce. Heated hard, it shreds, dries and loses its sweetness.

A soft-shell crab is a blue crab taken just after it moults, when it has backed out of its old shell and the new one is still soft. Crabbers hold peelers, crabs about to moult, in shedding tanks and lift them out within hours, before the new shell hardens. To clean one, cut away the face behind the eyes, lift the pointed sides of the top shell and pull out the gills, and remove the apron underneath. Then it is fried or sautéed whole and eaten shell and all.

Brennan's prints Louisiana lump crab on the Pecan Gulf Fish, where it crowns the day's fish with a pecan bordelaise, and in the Crab & Corn Omelette with roasted sweet corn and miso butter. Louisiana crab comes with the banana leaf-wrapped Gulf Fish en Papillote, crab joins the shrimp and oysters in the Seafood Gumbo, and the Louisiana Crab Claws come warm in a brown butter vinaigrette with fines herbes. Say lump, as printed, never jumbo lump, and never name a picking house.

Say aloud that the claws are served warm, so nobody expects a cold cocktail claw, and bring napkins and a plate for the shells: the guest holds the pincer, bites the meat and slides the cartilage out. Whether the claws can come chilled is a question for the chef, and shellfish questions always go to the kitchen.

faults.cause: The crabmeat went into the dish without being picked over.
faults.fix: Spread it thin on a cold tray and run your fingertips lightly through it, lifting out every hard flake.

faults.cause: The meat was stirred in early or worked too hard.
faults.fix: Fold it in at the very end with a spatula, lifting from beneath.

faults.fault: Dry, stringy crab with little sweetness
faults.cause: Already cooked crabmeat was cooked again over hard heat.
faults.fix: Only warm it through, gently, in butter or the sauce.

faults.fault: Claw meat that will not pull from the cartilage
faults.cause: Cooked cocktail claws were cooked a second time.
faults.fix: Warm the claws through and no more.

cards.front: What does the blue crab's Latin name, Callinectes sapidus, mean?
cards.back: Beautiful savoury swimmer: a crab of the brackish Gulf and Atlantic bays, blue in the claw and red when cooked.

cards.front: How much of the US blue crab catch does Louisiana land?
cards.back: About a quarter: Louisiana runs the largest blue crab fishery in the country.

cards.front: What is jumbo lump crabmeat?
cards.back: The two large muscles that drive the swimming legs, whole, white and costly, kept for dishes where the crab is the show.

cards.front: How does lump differ from jumbo lump and backfin?
cards.back: Lump is large body pieces and broken jumbo; backfin is smaller flakes with some body meat; jumbo lump is the two whole swimming muscles.

cards.front: How does claw meat differ from lump?
cards.back: It is darker, pinkish brown, firmer and sweeter, with a stronger flavour, and costs less; many cooks use it for stuffing.

cards.front: What is special grade crabmeat, and what is it for?
cards.back: White flake from the body, too small to count as lump; good for crab cakes, dips and stuffings.

cards.front: Why is picked crabmeat warmed and never cooked again?
cards.back: It is already cooked; hard heat shreds it, dries it and dulls its sweetness.

cards.front: How do you pick over crabmeat?
cards.back: Spread it thin on a cold tray and run your fingertips lightly through it, lifting out shell and cartilage without squeezing the meat.

cards.front: How do you add lump crab to a sauce or filling?
cards.back: Fold it in at the very end with a spatula, lifting from beneath rather than stirring, so the lumps stay whole.

cards.front: What is a soft-shell crab?
cards.back: A blue crab taken within hours of moulting, before its new shell hardens; cleaned, then fried or sautéed and eaten whole.

cards.front: What must you say when you describe the Louisiana Crab Claws?
cards.back: That they are served warm, in a brown butter vinaigrette, so nobody expects cold cocktail claws. They arrive cooked and are only warmed; bring napkins and a plate for the shells.

cards.front: Which grade does the Brennan's menu print, and what do you never claim?
cards.back: Louisiana lump crab, as printed; never claim jumbo lump, and never name a picking house.

questions.q: Which grade of crabmeat is the two large muscles that drive the swimming legs?
distractors: Lump
Backfin
Cocktail claw
questions.why: Jumbo lump is those two whole muscles, the costliest grade; lump is large body pieces, backfin smaller flakes, special white body flake.

questions.q: Which grade of crabmeat is darker, firmer and sweeter, and the least costly?
distractors: Jumbo lump
Lump
Backfin
questions.why: Claw meat is pinkish brown with a stronger, sweeter flavour and a firmer bite, and it costs less than the white body grades.

questions.q: A cook needs white crab flakes for crab cakes at a sensible price. Which grade fits?
distractors: Jumbo lump
Claw meat
Cocktail claws
questions.why: Special is white flake from the body: the right texture for a cake or a stuffing, without paying for whole lumps that would be broken up.

questions.q: Why is lump crabmeat only warmed through rather than cooked?
questions.answer: It is already cooked before it is picked
distractors: It is raw and must cook slowly to set
Heat turns it blue and bitter
It must stay cold to keep its shape
questions.why: Picked crabmeat is cooked before it is picked, so the kitchen only warms it; cooking it again costs texture and sweetness.

questions.q: What is the purpose of picking over crabmeat?
questions.answer: To lift out shell and cartilage
distractors: To sort the claws from the legs
To squeeze out the excess brine
To break the lumps into even flakes
questions.why: Even good crabmeat hides hard flakes; fingertips run lightly through a thin layer find them without crushing the lumps.

questions.q: How should lump crab go into an omelette filling or a sauce?
questions.answer: Folded in gently at the end
distractors: Stirred hard so it spreads evenly
Simmered in the sauce from the start
Blended smooth with the butter
questions.why: Lifting from beneath with a spatula at the last moment keeps the lumps whole; stirring or long cooking breaks them into shreds.

questions.q: When is a blue crab taken to be sold as a soft-shell crab?
questions.answer: Within hours of moulting, before the new shell hardens
distractors: Just before it moults, while the old shell is hard
In midwinter, when its shell is thinnest
Only once it has grown to jumbo size
questions.why: Crabbers hold peelers in shedding tanks and lift them out soon after the moult, while the new shell is soft enough to eat whole.

questions.q: Roughly what share of the US blue crab catch does Louisiana land?
distractors: About a tenth
Nearly all of it
About two thirds
questions.why: Louisiana runs the largest blue crab fishery in the country and supplies about a quarter of the national harvest.

questions.q: What should a server say aloud when describing the Louisiana Crab Claws?
distractors: That they are served on ice
That they come picked from the shell
That they come with a cocktail fork
questions.why: Guests often expect cold cocktail claws; ours come warm in a brown butter vinaigrette, so saying warm aloud avoids a surprise.

questions.q: Cocktail crab claws arrive from the supplier already cooked. How does the kitchen bring them to the table warm?
questions.answer: It warms them through and no more
distractors: It boils them again for ten minutes
It grills them until the shells char
It braises them slowly in the sauce
questions.why: Cooked a second time, the claw meat tightens onto the cartilage and will not pull free, so claws are only warmed through, or served cold.
